title: Project Launch
etis_alignment: ES-100 with selected ES-101 launch guidance
goal: Establish a credible engineering organization and evidence system before implementation complexity accelerates.
gate_question: Can the team operate with visible ownership, workflow discipline, AI governance, and repository structure before serious implementation begins?

expected_evidence.claim: A reviewer can understand the project, current direction, and evidence map.
Team purpose, cadence, expectations, and operating rhythm are explicit.
Student identities, GitHub identities, primary/backup ownership, and acknowledgements are explicit.
Communication, conflict handling, review, and definition-of-done expectations are explicit.
Allowed AI use, disclosure, verification, and human ownership are explicit.
Meaningful AI assistance is disclosed with human review/verification.
Project direction, Cycle 1 slice, assumptions, acceptance intent, and open questions have begun.
Initial scope, tasks, estimates, risks, schedule, and traceability have begun.
Consequential launch/scope/workflow decisions are durable and reviewable.

decisions_to_defend: Why this project and why this bounded Cycle 1 vertical slice?
Why are the team's role and backup assignments credible rather than ceremonial?
What is the team's definition of meaningful review before merge?
What AI use is acceptable, what is not, and what evidence makes accepted AI output trustworthy?
What evidence must exist before the team starts serious implementation?
What is explicitly out of scope and what business/engineering reasoning supports that boundary?

scenario_library.title: Executive Scope Pressure
scenario_library.prompt: A stakeholder asks the team to add authentication, notifications, and analytics before requirements are stable. Decide what you will do and defend the consequence.

scenario_library.title: AI Policy Under Pressure
scenario_library.prompt: A teammate used AI to draft requirements and code scaffolding but did not log it because 'we changed most of it.' Decide whether this is acceptable and what evidence is required.

scenario_library.title: Single-Point-of-Failure Teammate
scenario_library.prompt: One strong developer volunteers to own architecture, CI, deployment, and the database. The team says this is efficient. Decide whether to accept the model.

scenario_library.title: Perfect-Looking Empty Repository
scenario_library.prompt: The repository has every starter artifact completed with polished text, but there are almost no issues, decisions, questions, or review history. Is the team launch-ready? Defend your answer.

anti_patterns: Ownership with no backup or acknowledgement

title: Planning & Estimation
etis_alignment: ES-102 Requirements & Constraints; ES-103 Planning & Work Breakdown
goal: Convert reviewed requirements into visible, realistic, traceable, manageable work and explicit commitments.
gate_question: Can the team convert requirements into visible, realistic, traceable, manageable work before implementation accelerates?

expected_evidence.claim: The planning package is navigable and current.
In-scope/out-of-scope boundaries and Cycle 1 vertical slice are explicit.
Requirements connect to tasks, owners, estimates, evidence, and later verification.
Work is decomposed into reviewable units with ownership, dependencies, and completion evidence.
Estimates use ranges, assumptions, confidence, dependencies, and triggers.
Risks have triggers, probability/impact reasoning, mitigation, owner, and status.
The plan reflects actual capacity, dependencies, integration points, reviews, tests, and buffer.
Commitments are explicit and distinguish targets from assumptions.
The team knows what evidence will trigger a planning change.
Meaningful work has repository-visible intent, owner, outcome, and completion evidence.
Reviewed requirements, acceptance criteria, assumptions, and open questions remain current as planning decisions evolve.
Scope cuts, deferred work, technical debt, and consequential planning tradeoffs are recorded with rationale.
AI assistance used for requirements, planning, estimates, risks, or task decomposition is disclosed and human-reviewed.

decisions_to_defend: Why is this work decomposition small enough to estimate, review, and integrate?
What evidence supports the estimate range and confidence?
Which dependency has the highest schedule leverage and what happens if it slips?
What would cause the team to re-estimate or cut scope?
Which risk is most likely to invalidate the plan, and who owns the response?
What is a commitment versus an estimate, assumption, target, or optional item?
How does the plan preserve testing, review, and integration time rather than consuming it as buffer?

scenario_library.title: Fixed Date, Uncertain Scope
scenario_library.prompt: A stakeholder says the date cannot move, but the team has three high-uncertainty items and only one week of buffer. Decide what changes in the plan.

scenario_library.title: The 43-Hour Estimate
scenario_library.prompt: A teammate proposes a single 43-hour estimate because 'management needs one number.' Defend whether the team should use it and what to provide instead.

scenario_library.title: Dependency With No Owner
scenario_library.prompt: A critical feature depends on an external library the team has never used. It appears in the schedule but has no spike, owner, fallback, or risk trigger. What do you do?

scenario_library.title: AI Generated the Entire Plan
scenario_library.prompt: An AI tool produced the task plan, estimates, risks, and schedule in minutes. The plan looks plausible. What must humans do before it becomes engineering evidence?

anti_patterns: Risks are vague nouns without triggers/owners

title: Architecture & Review
goal: Make responsibilities, interfaces, data/context ownership, decisions, risks, governance, and failure boundaries reviewable before construction accelerates.
gate_question: What will be hard, risky, expensive, or unsafe to change later if this architecture is accepted now?

expected_evidence.claim: The architecture package is navigable and identifies the architecture baseline, major evidence, and unresolved review items.
System purpose, major components, responsibilities, dependency direction, and support for the Cycle 1 vertical slice are explicit.
The architecture diagram makes users, roles, components, interfaces, data stores, external services, trust/tool boundaries, and governance points inspectable.
Major component ownership, responsibilities, non-responsibilities, inputs, outputs, and evidence boundaries are explicit.
Important API and tool boundaries define inputs, outputs, errors, permissions, action limits, and consequences.
Authoritative and sensitive data, context ownership, visibility limits, AI/tool access, and logging expectations are explicit.
Important architecture decisions record alternatives, consequences, risks, assumptions, and ownership.
Architecture review findings, author responses, dispositions, owners, and follow-up actions are visible.
Architecture decisions have been reflected in scope, estimates, risks, schedule, task planning, and re-estimation where they changed the plan.
Important architecture risks, contracts, workflows, trust boundaries, and failure paths map to planned verification.
AI assistance used for architecture, diagrams, contracts, decisions, risk analysis, or review preparation is disclosed and human-verified.
Architecture review actions and consequential follow-up work are visible, owned, and traceable in repository workflow evidence.
Architecture changes and review responses are connected to visible repository review and change history where applicable.

decisions_to_defend: Where does each behavior belong?
What crosses a trust or data boundary?
What is intentionally coupled or decoupled and why?
What failure or scale assumption would invalidate the design?
Where must humans approve or override AI/tool action?

scenario_library.title: Quality Attribute Tradeoff
scenario_library.prompt: The team can improve availability, security, or delivery speed this cycle, but not all three. Choose and defend a proportional architecture decision.

title: Construction & Integration
etis_alignment: ES-106 Implementation Readiness; ES-107 Implementation; ES-108 Review & Integration; ES-109 Testing & Validation
goal: Prove controlled, reviewed, tested, traceable, AI-governed change.
gate_question: Why is this change safe enough to merge, and what evidence would make you change that judgment?

expected_evidence.claim: The construction, integration, review, AI-use, CI/CD, and test evidence package is navigable and current.
Implementation corresponds to traceable engineering intent and the accepted architecture.
Automated tests challenge important requirements, business rules, edge cases, boundaries, failure paths, and regression risks.
CI, manual, runtime, logging, or other verification evidence is preserved where it supports construction and integration claims.
Architecture review findings show what changed, what was deferred, and what evidence supports closure or continued risk.
Requirements and tasks connect to issues, branches, commits, pull requests, tests, CI results, and known limitations.
Pull requests consistently expose intent, issue linkage, evidence, risks, tests, and AI assistance for review.
Implementation work has repository-visible intent, ownership, requirement linkage, status, and completion evidence.
Meaningful changes show review comments, author response, status checks, risk discussion, and a merge or no-merge decision.
The configured CI workflow runs automated build/test checks on appropriate pull requests or branches and its limits are understood.
AI-assisted code, tests, reviews, documentation, debugging, or refactoring are disclosed with accepted/rejected output and human verification.
Construction, dependency, integration, AI, and release-readiness risks remain visible with owners, mitigations, and status.
Known limitations, deferred work, failed or incomplete evidence, and early release-readiness concerns are explicit.

decisions_to_defend: Why is this change scoped this way?
What review changed the implementation?
What did CI prove and not prove?
What dependency risk was introduced?
What AI-generated work was rejected or materially changed?

scenario_library.title: Green CI, Weak Evidence
scenario_library.prompt: All checks are green, but the new workflow has no negative or boundary tests. Is it merge-ready? Defend the decision.

anti_patterns: Green CI treated as complete proof

title: Cycle 1 Release
etis_alignment: ES-109 Testing & Validation; ES-110 Release Readiness
goal: Close Cycle 1 with a controlled, evidence-backed, honest release baseline and evidence-derived Cycle 2 handoff.
gate_question: What changed, what works, what evidence proves it, what risks remain, who owns them, and why is this release ready to present?

expected_evidence.claim: The Cycle 1 release package makes shipped scope, changed evidence since A4, the exact release baseline, release notes, known limitations, traceability, presentation evidence, and Cycle 2 handoff inspectable.
Final test, CI/CD, manual, runtime, and other validation evidence support the team's Cycle 1 release claims and disclose failed or incomplete checks.
Defects are classified by severity and disposition, with ownership, mitigation, deferral, and regression evidence where applicable.
Inspectible execution, manual, screenshot, log, or other verification evidence supports important release claims where useful.
AI assistance used for implementation, tests, documentation, release work, presentation preparation, or review is disclosed with human verification.
Known limitations and residual technical, user-facing, AI, security, and operational risks have explicit ownership, mitigation, disposition, and Cycle 2 implications.
Requirements connect through issues/tasks, branches or commits, pull requests, CI/CD, tests or evaluations, demo evidence, release notes, and the identified release baseline.
Cycle 1 implementation, defects, risks, and deferred work remain repository-visible with intent, ownership, status, and follow-up.
Release-relevant changes preserve visible review, verification, status checks, merge decisions, and traceability into the release.

decisions_to_defend: What exactly is in the release baseline?
Which claim is weakest?
What remains knowingly broken or limited?
Why is residual risk acceptable for Cycle 1?
What evidence should drive Cycle 2?

scenario_library.title: The Demo Works
scenario_library.prompt: The demo path works reliably, but two known defects and a missing regression test remain. Decide the release disposition and conditions.

anti_patterns: Cycle 2 becomes a feature wish list

title: Final Release & Maturity
etis_alignment: Evidence-selected ES-109 through ES-114, especially release, operations, monitoring, learning, and stewardship
goal: Show evidence-driven maturity improvement, operational readiness, governance, observability, recovery, stewardship, and final release defensibility.
gate_question: Can the team defend the final release as an evidence-driven maturity improvement, and can another engineer understand, operate, diagnose, recover, govern, and evolve the system within its documented limits?

expected_evidence.claim: The final release package identifies the exact controlled baseline, what changed during Cycle 2, known limitations, residual risks, traceability, maturity results, presentation evidence, and future stewardship.
Postmortem evidence, re-estimation, risks, scope decisions, task planning, and Cycle 2 maturity targets show why final improvement work was selected and what was completed, deferred, or cut.
Final unit, integration, system, regression, manual, AI validation, CI/CD, and runtime evidence support the team's final release claims and disclose failed or incomplete checks.
Final defects are classified by severity and disposition, with ownership, mitigation, deferral, and regression evidence where applicable.
Runbook, postmortem, failure modes, diagnosis, recovery paths, dependencies, operating assumptions, and supportability evidence are current and executable.
Logs, metrics, runtime behavior, failure signals, operational limits, and recovery indicators make important system behavior inspectable.
Permissions, approvals, sensitive-data handling, audit expectations, tool boundaries, governance controls, and residual security concerns are explicit.
Final AI assistance across implementation, tests, documentation, review, presentation preparation, and maturity work is disclosed with human acceptance, rejection, modification, and verification.

decisions_to_defend: What evidence from Cycle 1 justified each maturity target?
What materially improved during Cycle 2, and what evidence shows the intended risk reduction was actually achieved?
What can fail and how will an engineer know?
How is recovery performed?
What residual risk remains and who owns it?
How was AI-assisted final-release work independently reviewed or verified before the team trusted it?
Why does the identified final repository baseline support the claims the team is making about the release?
What would make you revoke or constrain the release?

scenario_library.title: Failure at 2 A.M.
scenario_library.prompt: A new engineer sees elevated errors and user complaints. Using only repository evidence, can they diagnose, contain, recover, and know whom to notify? Defend the final readiness state.

anti_patterns: Runbook cannot be executed by another engineer
Postmortem learning not connected to Cycle 2 work
